hard_constraints: Elya Rane dies in this scene; the damaged manifest fragment survives hidden behind the power-coupling housing.
Aevyn Soris uses weaponized Recognition (Jacen-derived Force-interrogation) — precise, intimate, controlled, not showy. He does NOT use crude torture or Sith lightning.
Aevyn extracts Ben's name, the fragment's existence, and the Iresh destination. He does NOT physically locate or recover the fragment chip.
Elya's POV ends with her death. The reader experiences the extraction through her procedural instincts and bodily sensation, not through Aevyn's internal monologue.
No ABY/BBY dating in narration or dialogue. Characters reference events directly ('after Caedus', 'before Shedu Maad').
No 'Legends' or 'Canon' as in-universe concepts. No Wookieepedia-style taxonomy.
Star Wars vocabulary: datapads not tablets, transparisteel not glass, durasteel not steel, turbolifts not elevators, comlinks not radios, blasters not guns.
'Jedi' is both singular and plural — never 'Jedis'.
'Darth' capitalized as a title before a name; generic 'the Sith' lowercase.
Capitalize 'Human'; lowercase 'galaxy'.
American English spellings throughout.
No real-world pop culture references, no film/book references, no out-of-universe authorial framing.
Force prose is experiential and mystical, never clinical. Avoid 'energy field' framing. Abilities surface as body-sensations first, named only after the body has felt them.
Aevyn's POV arc phase is 'lie_established' — he is already past the foundational corruption choice. No sympathy or backstory here; make the reader feel the wrongness of his method.
Elya should be competent, afraid, and briefly human before the plot kills her. The reader should feel that a decent person is being erased, not merely that an inciting incident has occurred.
The scene's dynamic is precise predator versus trapped bureaucrat: Elya is trying to hide what she sent and where, Aevyn is systematically taking it from her.
No paragraph contains more than one invented bureaucratic/technical term. Every technical phrase translates to immediate human stakes within two sentences.
Avoid 'system' as the default GAG metaphor; prefer logistics network, shipment trail, records chain, transfer chain, or operation.
Investigation vocabulary stays in physical thriller terms: fragment, duplicate manifest, quarantine disguise, archive, Foundation link, Iresh manifest/authorization.
No Mortis reference. No Crucible named on-page. No World Between Worlds. No High Republic. No sequel-trilogy entities. No kyber-bleeding mechanic. No Disney Mandalorian conventions.
'Ben' is unambiguously Ben Skywalker, never Ben Solo.
The One Sith remain in pre-emergence; no on-page appearance in this scene.
Vestara Khai is not mentioned in this scene.
Allana Solo / Amelia is not named or referenced in this scene.
Jaina Solo is not mentioned in this scene.
No Legacy comics future (Darth Krayt galactic war, Cade Skywalker) — excised entirely.
The Coruscant Jedi Temple is no longer Order property; the Order relocated to Shedu Maad in 44 ABY. This is not mentioned in this scene but must not be contradicted.
Elya's message to Ben uses an obsolete GAG-coded channel through his old service marker. The message text: 'GAG is still active. One of Jacen's last orders has two lives. Come alone. — E.R.'
The wrong approval field: Elya once quietly removed fourteen-year-old Ben's name from a GAG approval field because he was a child. This is the personal connection that motivates her message.
Aevyn's method kills by precision — pushing mind and body past survivable limits. It is not savage; the precision is what makes it morally and physically worse than crude torture.
Elya's procedural instinct is her only defense: keep talking, keep her hands visible, think in fields not bodies.

The fragment survives because Elya hid it by records instinct — not in the obvious terminal, not in any field Aevyn could read cleanly. It stays wedged behind the decommissioned workstation's power-coupling housing.

Setting: Coruscant, late night, third-floor records office of the Coruscant Bureau of Post-Conflict Logistics — narrow internal office, six workstations, no windows. Chrono reads 0233 at scene open, 0300 at close. Climate-control hum, terminal hum, recycled-air feel. After Aevyn enters: claustrophobic; no escape route Elya can reach in time.

Sensory details: recycled air tastes of old plasticrete and heat-stressed electronics. When Aevyn enters, Elya notices the absence of sound first: no footsteps, just the door-seal click and suddenly a man standing between her and the corridor.

Dialogue density target: medium. Interiority budget: max 250 words, max 3 paragraphs — Elya's procedural defense is spoken and behavioral; the extraction is experienced in the body, not narrated at length.
Opening mode: in medias res.
No new plot mythology introduced. No Iresh abstract description before it is physically clear in later chapters.
No theme as thesis. Put theme into behavior, pressure, cost, and consequence.
Maintain commercial reader-facing surface: goal, obstacle, movement, reversal, hook.
Explain only what the reader needs for the current emotional or plot decision. Keep exposition packets short (1-3 sentences). Return immediately to action, dialogue, or character reaction.
No paragraph contains more than one invented bureaucratic/technical term. Every technical phrase translated to immediate human stakes within two sentences.
Avoid 'system' as the default GAG metaphor; prefer logistics network, shipment trail, records chain, transfer chain, or operation.
canon_risks: Aevyn's weaponized Recognition must not be described as 'Sith magic' or 'dark side power' in narration — it is a Jacen-derived technique from Aing-Tii flow-walking fused with Force empathy, not a traditional Sith ability. The narration should not label it as dark-side; let the reader feel the wrongness through Elya's experience.
The obsolete GAG identity-address protocol must not be described as a 'dead-drop' in narration — use 'old service marker' or 'obsolete routing channel' to avoid anachronistic spy jargon.

Elya's death must not be described as 'her mind was torn apart' or similar clinical language — the Force prose rule requires experiential, mystical language. Describe the sensation from Elya's POV: pressure, clarity forced too fast, the feeling of memories being pulled to the surface, then the body failing.
The fragment must not be described as a 'data chip' or 'memory chip' — use 'fragment', 'manifest fragment', or 'the damaged copy' to stay in physical thriller vocabulary.

Aevyn must not be given any backstory or sympathetic detail in this scene. The scene card explicitly says 'avoid sympathy or backstory here; make the reader feel the wrongness of his method.' His POV arc phase is 'lie_established' — he is already past the foundational corruption choice.

Elya's procedural instinct must not be described as 'bureaucratic courage' or similar abstract label — show it through behavior: keeping her hands visible, talking in records vocabulary, buying seconds with the form of procedure.

The setting must not be described as 'the Bureau of Post-Conflict Logistics' in a way that implies it is a major institution — it is a narrow internal office, a small records office, not a named faction.
No reference to the Coruscant Jedi Temple or the Order's absence from Coruscant in this scene — it is not relevant to Elya's POV and would break the tight focus.
No reference to the Shedu Maad Memorial Foundation, the Vigil, Greyline, or any Act 2/3 organizations — this scene is the hook; the reader should not yet know the conspiracy's shape.
No reference to Iressa Vossk, Talon Veyr, or any character who has not yet been introduced.
Aevyn's lightsaber must not appear in this scene — he does not use it against Elya. His method is Recognition, not combat.
The word 'holocron' must not appear in this scene — the reader does not yet know about the unfinished holocron. The fragment points toward Iresh; the holocron is revealed later.
No reference to 'Holding' as a technique — only Recognition is used here. Holding is revealed later through Iressa's transmission.

Elya's death must not be sentimentalized or given a heroic last thought. The scene card says 'Elya dies as herself: practical, tense, and briefly human.' The reader should feel the loss of a specific ordinary person, not an inciting incident.
The fragment's survival must not be explained by Elya's conscious choice — it is 'records instinct', not a deliberate plan. She hid it by habit, not by design.

No reference to the 'wrong approval field' beyond the brief memory that motivates her message — the full story of that field is paid off in Chapter 2 when Ben remembers it. In this scene, it is a single emotional beat, not an exposition dump.
legends_continuity_notes: The Galactic Alliance Guard (GAG) was dissolved in disgrace after the Battle of Shedu Maad (41 ABY). Its records, infrastructure, and personnel were officially decommissioned. Elya's use of an obsolete GAG-coded channel implies the old machinery still has addresses for former members — a continuity detail that grounds the conspiracy in the afterlife of a real Legends institution.

Jacen Solo's Force odyssey (NJO through LotF) included study with the Aing-Tii (flow-walking), the Fallanassi (White Current), and Vergerean thought. Recognition is this novel's named extrapolation from that canon lineage — an inward turn of flow-walking fused with Force empathy. The technique is compatible with established Legends but was not previously named in published material.

The Battle of Shedu Maad (41 ABY) was the decisive engagement of the Second Galactic Civil War, where Darth Caedus was killed. The duplicated manifest dates from the final days before this battle — about six years before the novel's present (47 ABY).

Coruscant in 47 ABY: the Jedi Order has no institutional foothold. The Coruscant Jedi Temple was relinquished at the end of Fate of the Jedi (44 ABY) after the Senate voted to remove the Order following the Lost Tribe crisis. This is not mentioned in this scene but is the political context for Elya working in a mundane records office rather than a Jedi-affiliated institution.

The Bureau of Post-Conflict Logistics is a plausible minor Galactic Alliance administrative body — not a named Legends institution, but consistent with the post-war bureaucratic landscape described in the Fate of the Jedi and Crucible novels.

Elya Rane is a new character (not in published Legends), but her role as a former GAG records officer who quietly corrected a record to protect a child is consistent with the moral complexity of GAG personnel described in the Legacy of the Force novels — not all GAG members were complicit in the worst crimes.

The 'wrong approval field' is a new detail specific to this novel, but the practice of routing approvals through junior personnel to diffuse responsibility is consistent with the GAG's documented operational culture in the LotF series.

required_context_for_drafter: Elya's POV carries the entire scene. The reader experiences the extraction through her procedural instincts and bodily sensation, not through Aevyn's internal monologue.

The fragment is hidden behind the decommissioned workstation's power-coupling housing — a location Aevyn's mind-extraction does not reach because Elya hid it by records instinct, not by conscious plan. Ben finds it in Chapter 2.

Elya's message to Ben: 'GAG is still active. One of Jacen's last orders has two lives. Come alone. — E.R.' This message has already been sent when the scene opens.

This is the personal connection that motivates her to contact Ben now. It should be a brief emotional beat, not an exposition dump.

Aevyn enters without footsteps — just the door-seal click and suddenly a man standing between her and the corridor. This is the first sensory detail of his arrival.
Elya's procedural defense: keep talking, keep her hands visible, think in fields not bodies. She uses the vocabulary of records to buy seconds.

No sympathy or backstory for Aevyn in this scene. He is frightening before he is explained. The reader should feel the wrongness of his method.

The reader's first experience of the novel is sustained pressure — the Elya POV carries through Aevyn's arrival and her death without a chapter break.
